The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $T>0$, let $p_t$ be a strictly positive probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ for each $t\in[0,T]$, and let $q(s,x;t,y)$ be a jointly Borel, strictly positive transition density for $0\le s<t\le T$. Assume the marginal identity $p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx$ and the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity $q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz$ whenever $s<r<t$. For $0\le u<v\le T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx}{p_{T-u}(y)}\qquad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}),$$
and set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. This is the Bayes-reversed transition probability kernel from reverse time $u$ to reverse time $v$; its source state $y$ is the forward-time state at $T-u$ and its output $x$ is the state at $T-v$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
Elementary predictable Brownian integrands: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
Locally square-integrable predictable Brownian integrands.

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     Progressively measurable and predictable processes with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     Locally square-integrable predictable Brownian integrands,

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of Localized Ito integral. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion $d$-dimensional Brownian motion that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   Progressively measurable and predictable processes, with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of Localized Ito integral. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   Tonelli's theorem for nonnegative measurable functions on a sigma-finite product, applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   Locally square-integrable predictable Brownian integrands and
   Localized Ito integral the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   Continuous-time adapted processes and martingales for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   Localized Ito integral, clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   Localized Ito integral; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

No choice beyond the declared AC of the ambient interfaces enters the
construction: the coefficients $b,\sigma$ and the process are given data, and
the canonically localized integral is constructed in
Localized Ito integral. The Axiom of Choice is declared because the
conditional-expectation and $L^2$ interfaces used downstream assume it, and
the countable-choice obligations inherited from those interfaces are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume AC. Each input local martingale below is taken with everywhere-continuous adapted paths; it suffices that its full continuity event belongs to the initial sigma-algebra, so it can first be normalized there. All pathwise stopping operations use these representatives. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume AC. For nonnegative measurable $X_n$, $E[\liminf_n X_n\mid\mathcal G]\le\liminf_n E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely, in the extended sense. If real-valued measurable $X_n$ and $X$ satisfy $X_n\to X$ almost surely and $|X_n|\le W$ almost surely for one nonnegative $W\in L^1(P)$, then $E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]\to E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely and in $L^1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a finite signed
measure or a finite complex measure on the same measurable space. Then the
following are equivalent:

1. $\nu\ll\mu$;
2. for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta>0$ such that
   $$\mu(E)<\delta\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad |\nu(E)|<\varepsilon\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Put $C=C([0,\infty),\mathbb R)$, give $C$ the uniform-on-compacts topology,
and write $\pi_t(f)=f(t)$. Then
$$\mathcal B(C)=\sigma(\pi_t:t\ge0)=\sigma(\pi_q:q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)).$$
Here each expression on the right denotes the smallest sigma-algebra on $C$
making every displayed coordinate map measurable. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Fix $0\le s<T$ and $x$. Set $h_{s,x}(r,y)=q(s,x;r,y)/p_r(y)$ for $r>s$. The two classical forward equations and the exact adjoint product identity give $\partial_rh_{s,x}=D_rh_{s,x}$. This is $C^{1,2}$ in the evolving variables, because $p>0$ and both density solutions are classical; it requires no joint coefficient-derivative bound. On every closed interval $0\le u\le T-s-\delta$, [F2] applied after spatial localization gives $H^x_u=h_{s,x}(T-u,Z_u)$ a nonnegative local martingale. Its initial expectation is $\int q(s,x;T,y)dy=1$, since $Z_0$ has density $p_T$. Thus it is a supermartingale before $T-s$ by [F3]. This also applies at $s=0$, using the assumed transition density from forward time zero.

For any Borel $0\le f\le1$, put $H^f_u=\int p_s(x)f(x)H^x_u dx=B_{T-u,s}f(Z_u)$. Integrate each fixed-$x$ supermartingale inequality against $p_s(x)f(x)dx$, first tested on an arbitrary nonnegative bounded earlier-filtration event variable. Tonelli in [F3] proves the mixture supermartingale inequality without a common choice of conditional versions in $x$. The mixture lies in $[0,1]$. The complementary mixture $H^{1-f}$ is also a supermartingale and $H^f+H^{1-f}=1$ by the marginal identity, so both inequalities must be equalities. Hence $H^f$ is a true martingale on $[0,T-s)$, and $\displaystyle E B_{r,s}f(Z_{T-r})=\int p_s f\,dx$ for $s<r\le T$. Linearity extends this identity to bounded real Borel $f$.

Fix a compact smooth $f$ and put $F_\delta(r,y)=|B_{r,r-\delta}f(y)-f(y)|$. It is bounded by $2\|f\|_\infty$, and $\int p_rF_\delta(r,\cdot)\le E|f(X_{r-\delta})-f(X_r)|$. Integrating over any compact interior time interval and using continuity of $X$ and [F5] makes this tend to zero. On every compact time-state cylinder $p$ has a positive minimum, so $F_\delta\to0$ in local Lebesgue $L^1$. Apply [F4] to the occupation measure $\mu_n$ and the time-reversed function $F_\delta(T-u,y)$, first on a bounded state cylinder and then exhausting state balls; boundedness controls the tails of the finite measure $\mu_n$. Thus $\displaystyle E\int_a^bF_\delta(T-u,Z_u)1_{u\le\tau_n}du\to0$ for every compact interior $[a,b]$. Since $E(T-\tau_n)\to0$ and $F_\delta$ is uniformly bounded, [F5] removes stopping. No unknown marginal of $Z$ has been replaced by $p$ in this argument.

In the expectation identity in step 2.1 take $r=s+\delta$, multiply by any continuous time test $\zeta$ compactly supported in $(0,T)$, and integrate over $s$. Step 3.1, with $u=T-s-\delta$, permits replacement of $B_{s+\delta,s}f(Z_{T-s-\delta})$ by $f(Z_{T-s-\delta})$. Continuity of $Z$ and boundedness of $f$ then let $\delta\downarrow0$, giving $\int\zeta(s)E f(Z_{T-s})ds=\int\zeta(s)\int p_sf\,dxds$. Both integrands are continuous in $s$, the second because it equals $E f(X_s)$, so they agree at every interior time. Compact smooth tests determine finite Borel measures by [F6]. Continuity of both processes extends the equality to $s=0,T$. Thus $\operatorname{Law}(Z_{T-s})=p_s dx$ for every $s$.

Fix $0\le s<r\le T$. The conditional martingale identity of step 2.1 gives $\displaystyle E[B_{s+\delta,s}f(Z_{T-s-\delta})\mid\mathcal F^Z_{T-r}]=B_{r,s}f(Z_{T-r})$. Now step 4.1 supplies the law $p_{s+\delta}$ for the random argument on the left, so $\displaystyle E|B_{s+\delta,s}f(Z_{T-s-\delta})-f(Z_{T-s-\delta})|\le E|f(X_s)-f(X_{s+\delta})|\to0$. Continuity of $Z$ and the $L^1$ contraction in [F5] therefore prove $\displaystyle E[f(Z_{T-s})\mid\mathcal F^Z_{T-r}]=B_{r,s}f(Z_{T-r})$. First use compact smooth $f$, then [F6] extends to bounded Borel tests. The endpoint limit uses the marginal identity only after it has been proved in step 4.1.

Step 5.1 identifies all Bayes transitions of $Z$, and its initial law is $p_T$. The actual reversed process $Y$ has those kernels by [F1]. Iterated conditioning gives the same finite-dimensional laws; [F7] gives the same continuous path law. The Itô decomposition of $Z$ makes its compact-test compensated process a local martingale by [F2]. This property transfers to $Y$ in its natural filtration: its compensated tests are path-measurable functions of the continuous coordinate path and Borel time-state coefficients; stop each at its bounded-value hitting times, which are natural-filtration stopping times. The stopped local martingales are bounded, hence true, and their event-integral identities transfer by the equal path laws; unstop by exhaustion. This proves the stated local martingale problem for $Y$.

boundaries.evidence: For an empty Borel test set the mixture in Proof step 2.1 is zero. Proof step 6.1 still compares probability path laws, whose initial density p_T has mass one.
The zero test gives zero throughout2.1–step 5.1. The complementary test1 is essential:step 2.1 uses H^f+H^(1-f)=1 to make both nonnegative supermartingales true martingales.
Dimension d=1 requires no change in Proof step 1.1 Ito or3.1 occupation transfer. A one-point time choice s=r is approached only by the justified endpoint limit5.1.

No ellipticity is assumed by this conditional helper; occupation absolute continuity is an explicit Statement premise. Proof step 3.1 applies it to bounded functions on compact cylinders, avoiding an unsupported density claim for Z.

Proof step 1.1 allows s=0 and only evaluates classical q on r>s. Proof step 4.1 extends identified marginals to0,T by continuous paths, and5.1 reaches fixed s, including0, by its newly established marginal law.

AC is declared in Statement/A1. Proof step 2.1 integrates fixed-x event-tested inequalities by Tonelli, so it does not assume jointly selected conditional expectations; the auxiliary process is supplied, not selected as a maximizing comparator.

boundaries.reason: The conclusion is identification, not an iff. Proof3.1 first transfers local Lebesgue convergence to actual occupation;4.1 only then identifies p marginals. No reverse use of those marginals occurs.

No converse forward PDE theorem is asserted. Proof5.1 uses the already proved p marginals for its endpoint L1 estimate, and6.1 obtains equality of continuous path laws from actual Bayes conditional kernels.

risk_review.notes: Independently read all six proof steps. The quotient of the two classical forward densities solves the reverse space-time harmonic equation. Its nonnegative local martingales are supermartingales; integrating their event inequalities in x and using complementary positive mixtures summing to one gives true mixture martingales. Near-diagonal Bayes errors tend to zero in local Lebesgue L1 by continuity of the original forward path. Positive p on compact cylinders and the explicitly assumed stopped occupation absolute continuity transfer that convergence to Z; boundedness removes stops. Time averaging then identifies every marginal by continuity, before any auxiliary marginal is used in the endpoint conditional limit. Only afterward do L1 conditional contraction and pi-lambda give Bayes transitions and equal continuous path laws. Natural-filtration stopped compact-test martingales transfer by that equality. Endpoints follow from continuity and finite initial density. No circular auxiliary-marginal argument, initial moment or drift-square hypothesis is introduced. Occupation is an explicit intermediate premise whose applicability remains separately owed.
